stops.name: Bern, the light-quanta of March
stops.campa: Working evenings after his patent-office day, Einstein completes 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light,' proposing that light itself, however wave-like on the whole, arrives and is absorbed in discrete quanta of energy, not a continuous flood. It is the boldest paper of that year and the one he himself will call revolutionary; it explains the stubborn oddities of the photoelectric effect that classical wave theory cannot touch, and though almost no one accepts it at first, not even Planck, whose own quantum idea it extends, it is this paper, not relativity, for which Stockholm will one day give him the Nobel Prize.
stops.quote: According to the assumption to be contemplated here, when a light ray is spreading from a point, the energy is not distributed continuously over ever-increasing spaces, but consists of a finite number of energy quanta.
stops.quote_source: 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light,' Annalen der Physik, 1905

stops.name: Bern, the doctorate and the dance of the pollen grains
stops.campa: In the same burst of months Einstein finishes a doctoral dissertation determining molecular dimensions from the viscosity of sugar solutions, which the University of Zurich will accept, and a second paper explaining the jittering, random dance of pollen grains suspended in water, first noticed by the botanist Robert Brown eight decades before, as the visible fingerprint of the ceaseless bombardment of unseen molecules. Where philosophers still doubt whether atoms are anything more than a convenient fiction, Einstein gives a number that can be checked with a microscope and a stopwatch, and within a few years the last skeptics of atomic reality, Ostwald among them, concede the case is closed.
stops.quote: If the movement discussed here can actually be observed... then classical thermodynamics can no longer be looked upon as applicable with precision to bodies even of dimensions distinguishable in a microscope.
stops.quote_source: 'On the Movement of Small Particles Suspended in Stationary Liquids,' Annalen der Physik, 1905

stops.name: Bern, the electrodynamics of moving bodies
stops.campa: Einstein submits 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' known ever after as the founding paper of special relativity, though the word relativity appears nowhere prominent in its title. From two plain postulates, that physics looks the same to any observer moving at constant speed, and that light travels at one speed for all of them regardless of their own motion, he derives that time runs differently for observers in relative motion, that lengths contract, that simultaneity is not absolute. He needs no laboratory for it, only the clock tower he passes daily on his way to the patent office, and the discipline to follow the postulates wherever they lead.
stops.quote: The introduction of a 'luminiferous ether' will prove to be superfluous inasmuch as the view here to be developed will not require an 'absolutely stationary space.'
stops.quote_source: 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' Annalen der Physik, 1905

stops.name: Bern, does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy content
stops.campa: As an afterthought to the relativity paper, barely three pages long, Einstein works out that a body which radiates energy loses mass in exact proportion, and states the relation that will outlive every other sentence he writes: mass and energy are the same quantity measured two ways, mass merely a very concentrated store of energy, convertible in principle at the rate of the speed of light squared. He signs it still as a patent examiner, uncelebrated, in a Bern rented room; four papers in seven months, the photon, the atom's proof, the relativity of time, and this equivalence, remake physics from a desk that is not even a university's.
stops.quote: The mass of a body is a measure of its energy content.
stops.quote_source: 'Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?', Annalen der Physik, 1905

stops.name: Zurich, professor at the university
stops.campa: Four years after the miracle year, still slow to be recognized outside a small circle of physicists who write to him, Einstein is at last offered a chair, associate professor of theoretical physics at the University of Zurich, and leaves the patent office he has loved for its quiet. To Jakob Laub he jokes darkly about trading independence for academic rank; the pay, at first, is actually less than the patent office gave him, though the honor is greater. His students find him informal, unpretentious, given to interrupting his own lectures with, 'wait a moment, I have to think this over again' — a habit no professor before him had ever risked in front of a class.
stops.quote: So, now I too am an official member of the guild of whores.
stops.quote_source: Letter to a colleague on accepting the Zurich professorship, 1909

stops.name: Prague, the German University
stops.campa: A full professorship, better paid and more prestigious, draws the family to Prague and the German half of its divided university, where Einstein becomes, for the Austro-Hungarian bureaucracy's records, a subject required to declare a religion, and chooses, indifferently, 'mosaic.' He finds Prague society stiff with rank and small vanities that amuse him more than they trouble him, and works at the Institute for Theoretical Physics on the gravitational bending of starlight, publishing in 1911 the first, still-incomplete prediction that a ray grazing the sun should be deflected, a number later observers will need to correct, but the germ of the theory that will make him famous is already showing itself here.

stops.name: Brussels, the first Solvay Congress
stops.campa: Invited among the twenty-odd physicists Ernest Solvay gathers at the Hotel Metropole to argue out the crisis of the quantum, Einstein meets Marie Curie, Henri Poincaré, Max Planck, and Ernest Rutherford in one room for the first time, the youngest man there apart from a handful. He finds the proceedings, for all the illustrious names, oddly barren of real progress, a lament over the old physics's wreck rather than a plan for the new. Walking the corridors between sessions, he and Curie begin a friendship of mutual respect that lasts the rest of her life, two of the few unafraid to say plainly what they do not yet understand.
stops.quote: The Solvay Congress was on the whole a lamentation over the ruins of Jeans' theory. Nothing positive came out of it.

stops.name: Zurich, the return to the Polytechnic and Grossmann's tensors
stops.campa: Called back to Zurich, now as a full professor of the very Polytechnic that once made him wait a year to enter, Einstein turns in earnest to generalizing relativity to gravitation and accelerated motion, and finds the mathematics of curved space beyond what he was taught as a student. He appeals to his old classmate Marcel Grossmann, now a professor of mathematics, who introduces him to the tensor calculus of Riemann, Ricci, and Levi-Civita; the two co-author, in 1913, a first joint attempt at the field equations, still flawed, still years from the final form, but the mathematical language of general relativity is set from this collaboration onward.
stops.quote: Grossmann, you must help me, or I'll go crazy!

stops.name: Berlin, the call of the Prussian Academy
stops.campa: Max Planck and Walther Nernst travel to Zurich to persuade Einstein in person, and the offer they bring is unmatched: a salaried seat in the Prussian Academy of Sciences with no teaching duties at all, a research directorship, and a professorship at Berlin University he need only occasionally exercise. He accepts, arriving in Berlin in the spring of 1914 into the most prestigious scientific establishment in the German-speaking world, and into a marriage already failing; within months Mileva and their two sons return to Zurich, leaving Einstein alone in Berlin as Europe slides, that same summer, into general war.

stops.name: Berlin, the Manifesto to Europeans
stops.campa: When ninety-three of Germany's most eminent intellectuals sign a manifesto defending the war and denying German atrocities in Belgium, Einstein refuses, and instead puts his name, one of only four, to Georg Nicolai's counter-manifesto, the 'Aufruf an die Europäer,' calling on the educated of Europe to unite above the trenches rather than cheer them on. It is a nearly friendless position in wartime Berlin, and it will cost him socially for years, but it marks, publicly and for the first time, the pacifism and internationalism that will run beside the physics for the rest of his life.
stops.quote: Never before has any war so completely destroyed the fabric of international cooperation... it is a duty for educated, internationally minded Europeans at least to attempt to prevent Europe from suffering, as a result of this war, a fate similar to that which befell ancient Greece.
stops.quote_source: Manifesto to Europeans (Aufruf an die Europäer), October 1914

stops.name: Berlin, the field equations of November
stops.campa: Across four Thursday lectures to the Prussian Academy in November 1915, racing a rival calculation by the mathematician David Hilbert, Einstein corrects and finally completes the field equations of general relativity, the mathematics that ties the shape of space and time to the mass and energy within it. In the same days he applies the still-wet theory to a fifty-year puzzle, the small stubborn drift of Mercury's orbit that Newton's gravity cannot explain, and the new equations account for it exactly, to the decimal. He tells a colleague the discovery gave him heart palpitations; for days, he says, he could not work.
stops.quote: For a few days I was beside myself with joyous excitement.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arnold Sommerfeld, describing the Mercury calculation, December 1915

stops.name: Berlin, illness, divorce, and the marriage to Elsa
stops.campa: Worn down by wartime shortages and the strain of the theory, Einstein falls seriously ill in 1917 with stomach ailments that will trouble him for years, and is nursed back by his cousin Elsa Löwenthal, in whose Berlin apartment on the Haberlandstraße he has increasingly lived. His divorce from Mileva, agreed with brutal frankness, settles on her the money of a Nobel Prize he has not yet won but is already confident will come; weeks after the decree he marries Elsa, a companionable, undemanding match very unlike the partnership of physics that Mileva's had been.
